en: The Therāpadāna:
Pilindavaccha Chapter, 2.
The Apadāna of Thera Sela
“In the city of Haṃsavatī,
I was the master of the street;
having gathered my kinsmen together, I said:”
I spoke these words:
“A Buddha has arisen in the world,
an unsurpassed field of merit.”
He was the recipient of offerings for the entire world.
The khattiyas and the townspeople alike—
And the great householders and brahmins,
with confident hearts and joyful minds,
performed the duty of honoring the assembly.
Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors,
cavalrymen, and foot-soldiers—
With serene minds and joyful hearts,
They performed the communal rites:
the high-born, the princes,
the merchants, and the brahmins.
With serene minds and joyful hearts,
they performed the duties of the assembly;
so did the cooks and the barbers.
Bathers and garland-makers,
with confident hearts and joyful minds,
performed the duty of worship.
Washermen, weavers,
leather-workers, and barbers—
With hearts full of faith and joyful minds,
They performed their respective crafts:
fletchers, weavers,
leather-workers, and carpenters.
With serene minds and joyful hearts,
they performed the duty of honoring the community.
The smiths and the goldsmiths—
Likewise, those who offered gold leaf,
with hearts full of serene confidence and joyful minds,
performed the duty of honoring the Sangha.
Hired laborers, servants,
and many slaves and workmen,
each according to their own strength—
They performed their respective duties:
water-carriers, wood-gatherers,
farmers, and grass-cutters.
According to their own strength,
they performed the duties for the assembly;
they were flower-gatherers and garland-makers.
Those who were sellers of leaves and gatherers of fruit performed the duty for the community according to their own strength.
A courtesan, a slave-girl carrying water-jars,
a seller of cakes, and even a fisherwoman—
each according to her own strength.
They established a communal rule:
"Come, all of you, having gathered together,
let us form a single group."
"We shall perform our service in this unsurpassed field of merit.
Having heard these words of mine, they...
At that time, they bound the assembly together:
"Let them construct a well-made assembly hall for the community of monks."
Having completed that sal tree hall,
exultant and with a joyful mind,
surrounded by all of them, he—
I approached the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having approached the Perfectly Enlightened One,
the Lord of the World, the Bull among Men;
Having paid homage at the feet of the Teacher,
I spoke these words:
"O Hero, here are these three hundred..."
Groups of men from all sides offer you a well-constructed assembly hall, O Sage.
Having accepted it in the presence of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the One with Vision [spoke] before three hundred [monks].
He spoke these verses:
“The three hundred and Jeṭṭha as well followed along together.”
Having indeed created prosperity,
you shall all enjoy it.
When your final existence has arrived,
You shall touch the unsurpassed state of coolness,
the undecaying, deathless, and peaceful Nibbāna.
Thus the Buddha, the omniscient and unsurpassed, gave this explanation;
having heard the words of the Buddha,
I proclaimed my joy.
For thirty thousand eons,
I delighted in the world of the gods.
As Lord of the Gods, I exercised divine sovereignty five hundred times;
and a thousand times I was a king.
I was a wheel-turning monarch;
while I exercised sovereignty over the gods,
the great deities paid me homage.
Here, in this human kingdom,
there are assemblies and kinsmen;
when the final existence has been reached, [all these vanish].
There was a brahmin named Vāseṭṭha,
who possessed a hoard of eight hundred million; I was his son.
"Sela" is my name;
I have reached perfection in the six factors.
While wandering on foot for my exercise, I—
Honored by his disciples,
he approached an ascetic named Keṇiya, who was burdened by the heavy weight of matted hair.
Seeing the oblation prepared,
I spoke these words:
"Is it a wedding or a marriage?"
"Or have you been invited by a king?
"I desire to offer a sacrifice to the brahmins who are honored by the gods."
I do not invite the king;
no sacrificial offerings exist for me.
There is no marriage feast for me.
No marriage is found for me;
he who brings joy to the Śākyas is the best in the world, including the devas.
For the benefit and welfare of the entire world,
bringing happiness to all beings—
he has been invited by me today.
This is its preparation:
having the luster of the color of a *timbarūsaka* fruit,
immeasurable and incomparable.
The Buddha, peerless in form,
was invited for tomorrow;
like [a gem] struck by the blow of a furnace's mouth, he accepted.
Resembling glowing embers of khadira wood,
like a flash of lightning— this Great Hero,
the Buddha, has been invited by me.
Like a flame on the mountain peak,
like the full moon itself,
resembling the color of a reed-flame.
Thus I invited the Buddha—
the fearless one who has transcended fear,
the sage who brings about the end of existence.
The Great Hero is like a lion;
that Buddha has been invited by me.
He is skilled in the qualities of a Buddha.
He is invincible by others;
like a naga, he is a great hero.
That Buddha has been invited by me.
Skilled in practicing the true Dhamma,
the peerless Naga of a Buddha;
like a bull, the Great Hero.
Thus the Buddha was invited by me—
he of infinite beauty and immeasurable fame,
endowed with all the various marks.
The Great Hero is like Sakka;
that Buddha has been invited by me—
masterful, the leader of a group, and majestic.
Radiant and difficult to approach,
like Brahmā, that Great Hero—
the Buddha— has been invited by me.
The One of Perfect Dharma, the Ten-Powered One,
who has gone beyond strength and superior strength;
the Great Hero, like the earth.
Thus the Buddha was invited by me—
He who is strewn with waves of virtue,
and stirred by the consciousness of the Dhamma.
The Great Hero is like the ocean;
that Buddha has been invited by me.
He is difficult to approach and difficult to overcome.
Unshakable, exalted, sublime,
peerless, the Great Hero—
he, the Buddha, has been invited by me.
Of infinite knowledge, peerless and equal to none,
incomparable, having reached the pinnacle;
like the sky is the Great Hero.
Thus I invited the Buddha.
This is the fifteenth recitation section.
A refuge for those terrified by fear.
The refuge for those who go for refuge,
the consoler, the Great Hero—
he, the Buddha, has been invited by me.
The abode of the wise,
a field of merit for those seeking happiness,
a mine of jewels is the Great Hero.
Thus was the Buddha invited by me—
the one who brings comfort, the maker of wisdom,
the giver of the fruits of recluseship.
The Great Hero is like a cloud;
that Buddha has been invited by me.
He is the Eye of the World, possessed of great majesty.
The dispeller of all darkness,
like the sun, that Great Hero,
the Buddha, has been invited by me.
Among those liberated from objects,
the Sage who perceives intrinsic nature is like the moon, the Great Hero.
Thus the Buddha was invited by me—
the Buddha who has arisen in the world,
adorned with the [major] marks.
The Great Hero is immeasurable;
that Buddha has been invited by me—
he whose wisdom is immeasurable.
He whose virtue is incomparable,
whose liberation is peerless— he,
my Buddha, has been invited by me.
He whose wisdom is peerless,
whose strength is inconceivable,
and whose prowess is supreme—
Thus the Buddha was invited by me:
"Lust, hatred, and delusion—
all poisons have been utterly eradicated."
The Great Hero is like a medicine;
that Buddha has been invited by me.
[He is the remedy for] the many sufferings of the disease of the afflictions.
The dispeller of all darkness,
like a physician, that Great Hero—
the Buddha— has been invited by me.
O sir, this sound "Buddha," which you utter,
is indeed very difficult to encounter;
having heard "Buddha, Buddha," [one reflects:]...
Rapture arose within me.
Not being contained within,
that rapture surged forth from me.
With a joyful mind and at peace,
I spoke these words:
“Where indeed is that Blessed One?”
The eldest in the world, the bull among men;
having gone there, I shall pay homage to the giver of the fruits of recluseship.
Raising his right arm,
filled with joy and with palms joined,
he described to me the King of Dhamma.
"The dispeller of the dart of sorrow.
"Like a rising great cloud,
dark blue like collyrium,"
Behold this great forest appearing like the ocean;
it is here that the Buddha dwells.
The Sage is the tamer of the untamed;
he disciplines those who are to be disciplined and awakens them to the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Like one who is thirsty for water,
like one who is hungry for food,
or like a cow longing for her calf—
Thus I attended upon the Jina,
who was skilled in proper conduct and etiquette,
and possessed a restraint that was in harmony with the Dhamma.
I instruct my own disciples as they go into the presence of the Conqueror:
"The Blessed Ones are difficult to approach."
Like lions walking alone,
young men, you should come, placing one foot after the other.
Like a terrible venomous snake,
like the maned king of beasts,
like an elephant in rut with tusks.
Thus are the Buddhas difficult to approach;
they look with equanimity upon the sneezing and the spitting of the young brahmins.
Placing foot upon foot,
approach the presence of the Buddha,
honoring meditative seclusion.
Quiet and difficult to approach,
the Buddhas are hard to draw near;
they are venerable in the world with its devas.
When I ask a question or exchange greetings,
then be quiet.
Abide as sages.
That which the Fully Awakened One teaches for the attainment of the secure state of Nibbāna—
Attend to this very matter:
hearing the true Dhamma is bliss.
Having approached the Perfectly Awakened One...
I exchanged greetings with the Sage;
having concluded that conversation,
I examined his physical marks.
I had doubts about two of the marks,
yet I saw the thirty marks;
[I saw] the male organ sheathed in a sheath.
The Sage displayed this through his supernormal power.
Having extended his tongue,
he reached the openings of his ears and his nostrils.
I rubbed my forehead against his,
and the Jina covered it entirely;
having seen his marks, I—
When it was complete in both letter and spirit,
having reached the conclusion that he was a Buddha,
I went forth together with my disciples.
Accompanied by three companions,
I went forth into the homeless life;
before half a month had passed,
We have all attained Nibbāna,
having performed our work together in this unsurpassed field of merit.
Having wandered along one side,
they turned back on the other;
having laid down the rafters, they fell.
I dwelt in the communal rules of the Saṅgha;
by that well-performed deed,
I obtain eight benefits.
I am honored in all directions,
my wealth is immeasurable,
and I am a support for everyone.
Fear does not exist for me;
diseases do not exist for me,
and I preserve my long life.
I have smooth skin;
I dwell in a desired residence.
Having given eight rafters, I...
I dwelt in the Pūga-dhamma;
the attainment of the analytical knowledges and arahantship—
this was my eighth further goal.
One who has completed all that was to be done, whose task is finished and who is free from taints—
such a one is called "the eight rafters."
Your son was a great sage.
Having given five pillars,
I dwelt in the Dharma of the Saṅgha.
Through that well-performed deed,
I obtain five causes:
I am unshakable through loving-kindness.
I am one whose limbs are not deficient;
my words are worthy of being accepted,
and I do not boast as I am.
My mind is undisturbed,
and I am not harsh toward anyone;
by that well-performed deed, [may I attain peace].
I am pure in the Teaching;
respectful and deferential,
having done what was to be done, I am free from taints.
O Great Hero, your disciple,
that monk, O Sage, pays homage to you after having prepared a well-made seat.
I had a hall constructed;
by that well-performed deed,
I obtain five benefits.
Having been born into a noble family,
I became one of great wealth; I possessed every kind of prosperity.
Avarice does not exist in me.
When I desire to go,
a couch stands ready before me.
Together with that most excellent couch,
I go to my desired destination;
by virtue of that gift of a couch, [I have attained this].
I dispelled all darkness;
having attained the power of all direct knowledges,
the Elder, a sage, pays homage to you.
I accomplished all duties, both those of others and my own;
by that well-performed deed, [may I attain the fruit].
I entered the city of fearlessness.
When the sāla tree was fully completed,
I gave it away for communal use.
By that well-performed deed,
he attained preeminence.
Whatever tamers there are in the world, [he surpasses them all].
Those who tame elephants and horses,
having applied various methods,
tame them with cruelty.
It is not thus, O Great Hero,
that you have tamed men and women;
without punishment and without weapons.
The Sage, skilled in teaching, while praising the excellence of self-control and commending the virtue of generosity, spoke thus: "It is better to be one who controls oneself than one who does not."
While delivering a single question,
the Sage awakened three hundred people;
we have been tamed by the Charioteer.
Well-liberated and free from taints,
having attained all higher knowledges and powers,
they are extinguished through the destruction of the acquisitions.
In a hundred thousand aeons past,
whatever gift I gave then—
having transcended all fears, [I have attained this state].
This is the fruit of giving sal trees:
my defilements have been incinerated... [and so forth].
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me... [and so forth].
This is the teaching of the Buddha.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so forth].
“Such is the teaching of the Buddha.
Thus indeed the Venerable Sela, together with his retinue, recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One.
This is the second *apadāna* of the Elder Sela.
